A1.justification: Both PDFs describe L-SR1 by the same authors. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

before.justification: v1 reports original analytic optimization experiments, AMASS-trained human mesh recovery results on 3DPW, component ablations, and computational measurements.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds buffer sensitivity, learning-rate scalarization, reduced-data training, and inference-time secant-residual results.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and Figure 2 add the identity contribution to the direction, reconciling them with B0=I already specified in v1 Equation 7. Appendix B.2 introduces a separately trained scalarized learning-rate variant. The primary architecture and secant-penalized objective remain unchanged; PGSM mainly renames and clarifies the existing mechanism.

E1.justification: Both versions use random quadratics, the quadratic/Rosenbrock/Rastrigin benchmark suite, and AMASS-to-3DPW human mesh recovery. The added studies vary dimensions, hyperparameters, and training fractions within this retained coverage; they introduce no new dataset or task.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 expands the HMR comparison with reported TRACE, WHAM (ViT), and PromptHMR results, explicitly identifying their different training-data scope. It also adds L-SR1 without the secant penalty to the HMR comparison. The analytic comparator set remains unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 adds systematic training/evaluation buffer sweeps, unroll-depth and secant-weight sweeps using a 50-step loss summary, separately meta-trained scalar/vector controls, and AMASS training fractions from 80% to 0.1%. These substantially expand experimental design within existing tasks; the retained benchmark settings are largely unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's projection and input/width ablations, v2 adds buffer robustness, cross-dimensional hyperparameter sensitivity, scalar versus coordinate-wise learning-rate comparisons, and data-efficiency studies. Section 5.2.2 also directly measures whether the training penalty improves secant consistency during HMR inference.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly documents four random seeds for the new quadratic studies and mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting in Table 3. Conversely, the retained input/width ablation loses all uncertainty values from v1 Table 3 to v2 Table 4. No increase in runs for the legacy results is established.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results, including sensitivity heatmaps, secant-residual trajectories, scalarization comparisons, and reduced-data HMR scores: 53.03 with 10% AMASS and 70.78 with 0.1%. The new no-secant HMR row reports 52.80. Headline results remain 51.58 for L-SR1, 51.74 at four steps, and 55.90 for LGD.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 adds the mathematical qualification that coordinate-wise rate scaling can make the effective operator nonsymmetric, so the PSD argument alone does not guarantee descent. v2 also corrects QN/SR1 update indexing and relaxes the stated sufficient condition on B0 from positive definite to semidefinite. Appendix F retains the existing lemma and proof.

C1.justification: v1's contribution statement and conclusion describe a projection enforcing the secant condition. v2 instead claims PSD construction with training that encourages approximate secant consistency. It also removes the faster-global-minimum claim and narrows the intended advantage to costly iterative objectives, substantially qualifying the central guarantees and scope.

C2.justification: v2 explains dimension-dependent loss summaries, interprets scalarization's differing effects on quadratics and HMR, and distinguishes four-step speed from best-error inference cost. Appendix D adds task-distribution dependence, possible retraining, and hyperparameter limitations. The earlier HMR caption's inference about better internalized 3D priors is removed.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a project/code URL where v1 only promises release upon acceptance. It newly documents tensor shapes, coordinate sharing and BatchNorm operations, Bernoulli confidence sampling, LBFGS without explicit line search, and timing scope. Most architecture tables, hardware information, and training hyperparameters were already present.

R1.justification: v2 adds Chen et al. (2022), Liao et al. (2023), and Metz et al. (2022, 2023), and distinguishes its mechanism from online learned preconditioning. These refine the existing learned-optimization positioning; bibliographic corrections and citation-style changes do not constitute additional research coverage.

P1.justification: The abstract, motivation, mechanism explanation, experimental narrative, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Learned projection becomes PGSM, performance-profile definitions move to Appendix C.2.2, HMR gains dedicated evaluation and diagnostic subsections, and Appendix B is reorganized into four analyses.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main-text layout, revises the block diagram, separates the retained performance-profile panel into Figure 4, and adds heatmaps and a secant-residual plot. HMR curves gain another comparator, while Table 1 is substantially restructured around training scope and timing; model sizes move to Appendix A.

improvement.justification: v2 resolves an important mismatch between v1's claimed secant guarantees and its penalty-based method, explicitly qualifies descent reasoning, and adds direct mechanism diagnostics and controlled robustness studies. Clearer HMR timing and training-scope comparisons improve interpretation. Removing uncertainty from the retained input/width ablation is a localized regression, outweighed by the stronger validation and more defensible central claims.
